story: In 1917, young women were hired at factory studios to paint glow-in-the-dark watch dials with luminous radium paint. To keep the tiny numerals sharp, supervisors instructed the painters to point their camel-hair brushes between their lips. Believing the material was completely safe, workers painted their teeth, nails, and faces to glow in the dark for fun. Meanwhile, plant managers and scientists wore lead masks and used protective tongs. Ingested radium mimicked calcium in the body, depositing directly into the workers' bones and causing painful decay known as radium jaw. When painters fell ill, company executives denied responsibility and attempted to smear the women by claiming they had syphilis. In 1927, five dying dial painters sued United States Radium Corporation. Their landmark lawsuit and 1928 settlement established a crucial legal precedent allowing American workers to sue employers for occupational health hazards.
angle: Factory workers were encouraged to sharpen radium paintbrushes with their lips while company bosses used lead shields and tongs to protect themselves.

claims.claim: Female factory workers applied radioactive luminous radium paint to watch, clock, and instrument dials.
Supervisors instructed the dial painters to sharpen paintbrushes between their lips and tongues using a technique called lip-pointing.
Factory management told the workers that the radium paint was completely harmless to their health.
Company executives and scientists avoided radium exposure themselves by using lead screens, masks, and tongs.
Believing the radium paint was safe, workers painted their fingernails, teeth, and faces to make them glow in the dark.
Dial painters earned about one and a half cents per dial, painting around 250 watch faces per shift.
The human body mistook ingested radium for calcium, absorbing and depositing it directly into the bone structure.
Ingesting radium caused bone destruction, loose teeth, severe anemia, and jawbone decay known as radium jaw.
United States Radium Corporation attempted to conceal the truth and falsely attributed worker illnesses to syphilis.
Five New Jersey dial painters—Grace Fryer, Edna Hussman, Katherine Schaub, Quinta McDonald, and Albina Larice—filed a lawsuit against United States Radium Corporation.
The New Jersey lawsuit settled in autumn 1928, providing each woman $10,000 plus an annual annuity and payment for medical and legal expenses.
The Radium Girls litigation established key legal precedents enabling individual workers to sue corporations for labor abuse and occupational diseases.

disputed: Company management claimed worker deaths were caused by syphilis or non-industrial infections; the script should frame these claims as corporate cover-up tactics disproven by medical investigations.
Specific timelines and payout outcomes varied across regional plants (New Jersey vs. Illinois); the script should focus on the 1928 New Jersey settlement as the primary legal turning point.
